questions.q: What is the core tension this lesson covers at the containment-strategy level?
options: There is no real tradeoff between speed and evidence preservation in practice
Containing fast (e.g., powering off a machine) can destroy evidence that containing carefully would have preserved
Containment and evidence preservation are always the exact same action
Evidence preservation is only ever relevant after eradication is already complete
questions.explain: The fastest-looking containment move, like powering off a machine, can destroy volatile evidence that a slower, more careful approach would have kept.

questions.q: According to the lesson, which situations make formal evidence preservation matter, beyond just curiosity about what happened?
options: Only incidents involving a single low-severity false positive
Only incidents that happen during business hours
Evidence preservation never actually matters in any real incident
Potential legal action, regulatory reporting requirements, and cyber insurance claims
questions.explain: Legal action, regulatory breach-notification requirements, and insurance claims are real categories where proving what happened has formal consequences.

questions.q: What is the correct order of operations described for containing while preserving evidence?
options: Isolate the host (not power it off), acquire a memory dump and disk image, then move into eradication and rebuild
Eradicate and rebuild first, then isolate the host
Power off the host immediately, then worry about evidence afterward
Acquire evidence only after the system has already been rebuilt
questions.explain: Isolating keeps the machine live so nothing in memory is lost, and evidence is captured before eradication destroys it.

questions.q: Why does the lesson emphasize recording a cryptographic hash and a chain of custody for captured evidence?
options: So anyone later can verify the evidence hasn't been tampered with since it was captured, which matters if it faces outside scrutiny
Chain of custody is only relevant for physical evidence, never digital evidence
A hash is only needed if the evidence will never be reviewed by anyone else
Hashing and chain-of-custody documentation are purely optional formalities with no practical use
questions.explain: A documented, verifiable chain of custody is what lets evidence hold up to scrutiny from a regulator, court, or insurer later.

questions.q: In the healthcare breach example, what would the organization have lost if it had wiped and rebuilt the server immediately instead of imaging it first?
options: The ability to isolate any future compromised system
The server's hardware warranty
Nothing — rebuilding immediately has no real downside in a HIPAA-regulated environment
The ability to later prove exactly what the attacker could and couldn't access, which regulators and outside counsel needed months afterward
questions.explain: Without the preserved memory dump and disk image, the organization would have no way to prove the scope of what was accessed when later asked.
